{{Short description|Interval of binary floating-point numbers with a common sign and exponent}}
[[File:Binade.svg|thumb|alt=An axis with tick marks for each floating-point number between 0 and 1 with 3 bits of precision and minimum exponent &minus;5, with an underbrace labelled +1.xy &times; 2^(&minus;2) to highlight the ticks for numbers from 1/4, inclusive, to 1/2, exclusive.|The binade of exponent &minus;2 in the floating-point numbers with 3 bits of precision and minimum exponent &minus;5]]

In [[software engineering]] and [[numerical analysis]], a '''binade''' is a set of numbers in a binary [[Floating-point arithmetic|floating-point format]] that all have the same sign and exponent.
In other words, a binade is the [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]]
<math>[2^e, 2^{e + 1})</math> or <math>(-2^{e + 1}, -2^e]</math>
for some integer value&nbsp;<math>e</math>, that is, the set of real numbers or floating-point numbers <math>x</math> of the same sign such that
<math>2^e \leq |x| < 2^{e + 1}</math>.<ref name="handbook">{{cite book

Some authors use the convention of the closed interval <math>[2^e, 2^{e + 1}]</math> instead of a half-open interval,<ref>{{cite journal

|number=3

|publisher=IEEE

|issn=0018-9162
}}</ref>
sometimes using both conventions in a single paper.<ref>{{cite conference

|pages=42–49
|doi=10.1109/ARITH.2015.27
|issn=1063-6889
}}</ref>
